sources.title: Records of the Grand Historian, Han dynasty, volume I
sources.note: University-press translation record checked for Sima Qian, authorship, compilation period, work scope, adjacent peoples, and the text’s historical and literary character.

sources.title: A History, Forgotten and Recreated: Yan expansion and the Donghu in the Shiji
sources.note: Peer-reviewed historiographical study checked for the retrospective construction of Yan expansion and warnings against finding one archaeological Donghu ethnicity from the Shiji story.

sources.title: Dong Hu tribal confederation
sources.note: Scholarly reference entry checked for textual attestations, political description, geographic setting, later defeat, and historiographic uncertainty.

sources.title: Notes on the Donghu
sources.note: Scholarly article record checked for early Chinese textual references, Donghu research history, archaeological proposals, and the limits of later descent narratives.

sources.title: Warring States Political History
sources.note: Cambridge history chapter checked for territorial-state growth, household registration, mass armies, diplomacy, scarce writing, and the partisan character of surviving texts.

sources.title: Ancient China and Its Enemies
sources.note: Cambridge book record checked for study scope, early Chinese frontier categories, nomadic power, and the need to analyze textual representations historically.

sources.title: Arrival and transformation of nomadic culture in the upper Liao River: Jinggouzi culture
sources.note: Peer-reviewed study checked for mixed Jinggouzi assemblages, horses, sheep, cattle, pigs, weapons, interaction, hierarchy, and explicit uncertainty over identification with Donghu.

sources.title: Genetic data suggests that the Jinggouzi people are associated with the Donghu
sources.note: Peer-reviewed open record checked for forty-two sampled remains, uniparental markers, proposed Donghu association, pastoral interpretation, and small-sample limitations.

sources.title: Staging and Chronology of Archaeological Cultures in the Liaoxi Mountainous Region
sources.note: Scholarly regional chronology checked for Upper Xiajiadian phases, distribution, debated dates, later Yan influence, and archaeological classification limits.

sources.title: A grave matter: pastoral economies and identities in Upper Xiajiadian culture
sources.note: Peer-reviewed publication record checked for mortuary variability, pastoral transition, group identities, and the danger of treating an archaeological culture as a single people.

sources.title: Genetic diversity in the ancient human population of Upper Xiajiadian culture
sources.note: Peer-reviewed genetic study checked for West Liao River population structure, differing subsistence patterns, and limits on converting sampled ancestry into ethnic labels.

sources.title: Settlement Patterns in the Chifeng Region
sources.note: Long-term regional survey checked for settlement visibility, millet remains, mixed farming and grazing, environmental context, and uncertainty about highly mobile models.

sources.title: Human subsistence strategies and climate change in the Bronze Age West Liao River Basin
sources.note: Peer-reviewed study checked for radiocarbon dates, floated plant remains, site distributions, millet, pastoral change, and environmental interpretation.

sources.title: Ancient genomes from northern China suggest links between subsistence changes and human migration
sources.note: Peer-reviewed study checked for West Liao River ancestry shifts, millet and pastoral economies, migration, and the distinction between biological ancestry and named peoples.

sources.title: The Archaeology of the Chinese Bronze Age
sources.note: University-press archaeological synthesis checked for northern interaction zones, chronology, metallurgy, settlements, graves, and material-culture comparisons.

sources.title: Chronological and Cultural Framework of Bronzes in Northern China
sources.note: University dissertation checked for northern bronze chronology, Jinggouzi and Upper Xiajiadian attributions, weapons, ornaments, and competing ethnic interpretations.

sources.title: Metals and society on the eastern Eurasian steppe
sources.note: Scholarly collected volume checked for Dajing copper mining, molds, northern metallurgy, exchange, and caution in attaching artifacts to named groups.

sources.title: Early Pastoral Economies and Herding Transitions in Eastern Eurasia
sources.note: Peer-reviewed synthesis checked for regional herding transitions, habitation evidence, horses, mobility, and rejection of one timeless nomadic package.

sources.title: Dairy pastoralism sustained eastern Eurasian steppe populations for 5,000 years
sources.note: Peer-reviewed proteomic study checked for ruminant dairy, later horse milk, temporal differences, and what dental calculus can and cannot establish.

sources.title: Origins of equine dentistry
sources.note: Peer-reviewed record checked for directly dated horse-tooth intervention, changing bits, veterinary observation, and chronological limits.

sources.title: Intensification in pastoralist cereal use and trans-regional networks
sources.note: Peer-reviewed isotope and archaeobotanical study checked for uneven millet use, exchange networks, and regional chronological variation.

sources.title: A Dynamic 6,000-Year Genetic History of Eurasia’s Eastern Steppe
sources.note: Peer-reviewed genomic study checked for repeated mixture, diverse ancestry, later Xiongnu formation, and limits of projecting political identities onto genes.

sources.title: Bronze Age Mongolia
sources.note: Oxford Handbook chapter checked for changing pastoralism, mobility, monuments, chronology, settlement scarcity, and debated social complexity.

sources.title: Nomadic Art of the Eastern Eurasian Steppes
sources.note: Museum scholarly catalogue checked for northern Chinese objects, portable animal art, horse equipment, exchange, and the absence of indigenous written records.

sources.title: Deer Stone Monuments and Related Bronze Age Sites
sources.note: UNESCO documentation checked for 1200 to 600 BCE monument landscapes, horse deposits, carving, ritual gathering, distribution, and chronology.

sources.title: The Mongolian Deer Stone-Khirigsuur Complex
sources.note: Smithsonian excavation synthesis checked for graves, horse offerings, hearths, feasting remains, preservation, and interpretive limits.

sources.title: Socially Integrative Facilities and Societal Complexity on the Mongolian Steppe
sources.note: Scholarly chapter checked for how monuments coordinated dispersed communities without automatically implying a centralized territorial state.

sources.title: Palaeopathological analysis of skeletal remains from Bronze Age Mongolia
sources.note: Peer-reviewed record checked for the small skeletal sample, trauma, joint changes, visible disease, riding interpretation, and preservation limits.

sources.title: The Khanuy Valley Project on Early Nomadic Pastoralism
sources.note: Smithsonian field-project account checked for habitation-search methods, households, animal remains, plants, sediments, camp organization, and domestic-site visibility.

sources.title: A Sketch of the Earliest Mongolic Language
sources.note: Peer-reviewed study checked for the sixth- and seventh-century CE Bugut and Khuis Tolgoi inscriptions, far later than the Donghu atlas interval.

sources.title: Hou Han Shu: Biographies of the Wuhuan and Xianbei
sources.note: Later transmitted Chinese history checked for the dedicated Wuhuan and Xianbei biography, descent claims, social descriptions, and its much later date.

sources.title: Petroglyphic Complexes of the Mongolian Altai
sources.note: UNESCO documentation checked for multi-period scenes of hunting, herding, carts, riders, environmental change, and the limits of identifying depicted peoples.

sources.title: Heterarchy and Hierarchy among the Ancient Mongolian Nomads
sources.note: Scholarly study checked for later Donghu defeat traditions, Wuhuan and Xianbei descent accounts, family and kin groups, leadership, and political reorganization.

sources.title: Shiji: Biographies of the Xiongnu, Chinese text view
sources.note: Transmitted textual passage and historical commentaries checked for the characters 東胡, location north of Yan, leaders, later power, and retrospective interpretations.

sources.title: Qian Han Ji: Annals of Emperor Xiaowu 2
sources.note: Transmitted historical parallel checked for the later Modu and Donghu demands narrative, land dispute, attack, and its retrospective framing.

sources.title: Archaeological cultures and Shanrong-Donghu in Liaoxi, ninth to third centuries BCE
sources.note: Peer-reviewed article record checked for Upper Xiajiadian and Jinggouzi comparisons, Shanrong and Donghu interpretations, Liaoxi geography, chronology, and disputed ethnic attribution.

sources.title: Dong Hu tribal confederation, DOI record
sources.note: Scholarly reference entry checked specifically for confederation terminology, the danger of a singular political or ethnic model, geographic range, and historiographic uncertainty.

proposedOverrides.name: Donghu peoples in early Chinese histories
proposedOverrides.summary: “Donghu” is a Chinese exonym, not a recovered self-name or single archaeological culture. Its inaccurate atlas endpoint predates the famous Xiongnu defeat by more than a century.
